ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Heat the oven to 285°F (140°C). Warm the milk and cream with the split vanilla pod and its seeds until steaming, then take off the heat and leave to infuse 10 to 15 minutes.
Whisk the yolks with the sugar just until pale; do not beat in air. Pour the warm cream over them slowly, stirring, then strain out the pod.
Pour into 4 shallow ramekins and set them in a deep tray. Add hot water to come halfway up the sides.
Bake 35 to 45 minutes, until the edges are set and the centres still tremble. Cool, then chill at least 3 hours or overnight.
Just before serving, scatter the brown sugar thinly over each and caramelize with a kitchen torch, or 1 to 2 minutes under a very hot grill. Let the crust harden 1 to 2 minutes.

nutritionHighlights.note: Four yolks across four ramekins give each serving a good share of the day's choline.
Cream and yolks both carry vitamin A, which needs the fat around it to be absorbed.

recipes.curationNote: Proportions follow Géraldine (4 yolks, 50 g sugar, milk and cream, a vanilla pod, a water bath at 140°C). Wikipédia confirms the yolk, sugar, cream and vanilla custard with cassonade on top, first written down by Massialot in 1691.

recipes.name: Mousse au Chocolat
recipes.flavorProfile: Deep, slightly bitter dark chocolate made light by beaten egg whites, cool and airy on the tongue and dense at the bottom of the glass.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat; dark chocolate brings iron, magnesium and cocoa flavanols, and the eggs add protein, but the raw eggs mean very fresh eggs, and none for pregnancy or anyone immune-compromised.
instructions: Melt the chocolate gently over barely simmering water, or in short bursts in the microwave, and let it cool to just warm, about 5 minutes.
Stir the yolks and vanilla into the chocolate one yolk at a time until glossy.
Whisk the whites with the salt to soft peaks, then add the sugar and keep whisking to firm, glossy peaks.
Stir a third of the whites into the chocolate to loosen it, then fold in the rest gently in two additions until no white streaks remain.
Spoon into 4 glasses or one bowl and chill 2 to 4 hours, until set.

nutritionHighlights.note: Dark chocolate is one of the richer everyday sources of magnesium.
The chocolate carries a fair amount of non-heme iron.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine gives 4 eggs to 150 g dark chocolate with a little sugar and no cream, which is the classic French home mousse. Wikipédia describes it as chocolate lightened with beaten whites, recorded by Menon in 1755.

components.note: one round of shortcrust, rolled to fit the pan

recipes.name: Tarte Tatin
recipes.flavorProfile: Apples cooked down in dark butter caramel until soft and amber, turned out over a crisp pastry base, sweet with a burnt-sugar edge.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat with a lot of sugar and butter; the apples bring some fibre and potassium, and a thin slice is plenty.

ingredients.cutPrep: about 6 firm apples, peeled, cored and quartered

instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Roll the pastry into a round a little wider than a 26 cm ovenproof skillet and chill it while you make the caramel.
Spread the sugar in the dry skillet over medium heat and leave it to melt and turn amber, 6 to 8 minutes, swirling rather than stirring. Take off the heat and stir in the butter.
Pack the apple quarters in tightly, rounded side down, in concentric circles. Return to medium heat and cook 10 to 15 minutes, until the juices bubble and darken.
Lay the pastry over the apples and tuck the edge down inside the pan. Prick it a few times.
Bake 45 to 50 minutes, until the pastry is deep golden. Rest 5 to 10 minutes, then lay a plate on top and turn the tart out in one move. Serve warm, with crème fraîche if you like.

nutritionHighlights.note: About six apples go into the tart, so each slice carries some fibre.
The cooked apples hold their potassium.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine bakes 6 apples in a dry caramel of 120 g sugar and 50 g butter in a 26 cm pan at 180°C, then turns it out. Wikipédia names the Tatin sisters at Lamotte-Beuvron and allows puff, sablée or brisée pastry; the shortcrust base is used here.

components.note: about half a batch, rolled 3 mm thin

recipes.name: Tarte Fine aux Pommes
recipes.flavorProfile: A crisp, shattering sheet of puff pastry under fanned, paper-thin apple slices with caramelized edges and a buttery sugar glaze.
recipes.healthBenefit: A treat made of butter pastry and sugar; the thin layer of apple adds a little fibre and potassium.

ingredients.cutPrep: about 3 apples, peeled, cored and sliced 2 mm thin
juice only, to keep the apples pale

instructions: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Roll the puff pastry 3 mm thin, cut a 28 cm round or a long rectangle, and lay it on a lined tray. Prick it all over and chill 15 minutes.
Toss the apple slices with the lemon juice. Overlap them in tight rows or a rosette, leaving a 1 cm border.
Brush the apples and the border with the melted butter and scatter the brown sugar over.
Bake 25 to 35 minutes, until the pastry is puffed and deep golden and the apple edges have browned. Serve warm.

nutritionHighlights.note: The apple slices add a modest amount of fibre.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine bakes thin apple slices and brown sugar on puff pastry at 180°C, with a layer of applesauce under them. Wikipédia describes the apple tart on puff or brisée pastry. The tarte fine is the thin version with no compote, only apples, butter and sugar, so the compote is left out here and the oven is hotter to crisp the thin sheet.

recipes.name: Clafoutis aux Cerises
recipes.flavorProfile: Dark sweet cherries baked into a soft, eggy, lightly sweet batter, somewhere between a flan and a pancake, with a faint almond note from the pits.
recipes.healthBenefit: Lighter than most French desserts, made with milk rather than cream; the cherries bring vitamin C and polyphenols and the eggs and milk add protein and calcium.

ingredients.cutPrep: stemmed, pits left in as in Limousin

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached
Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Butter a 23 cm baking dish and dust it with the 10 g of sugar.
Spread the cherries in the dish in one layer.
Whisk the eggs with the 75 g sugar and salt, then whisk in the flour until smooth and add the milk a little at a time until the batter is thin.
Pour the batter over the cherries and bake 35 to 40 minutes, until puffed and golden and set in the centre.
Serve warm or at room temperature, warning everyone about the pits.

nutritionHighlights.note: Half a kilo of cherries gives each serving some vitamin C.
The milk in the batter adds calcium.
Three eggs and the milk give it more protein than a cake.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine bakes 500 g cherries in a batter of 3 eggs, 100 g flour, 75 g sugar and 300 ml milk at 175°C. Wikipédia places it in Limousin and notes the cherries traditionally keep their pits, which add flavour; that is kept here.

recipes.name: Crêpes Suzette
recipes.flavorProfile: Thin warm crêpes folded into quarters and soaked in a glossy orange butter caramel, bright with zest and warmed by orange liqueur.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat of butter, sugar and liqueur; the orange juice brings a little vitamin C, and the alcohol mostly stays if it is not flamed for long.

ingredients.cutPrep: zest finely grated, then juiced, about 100 ml

instructions: Cook 8 thin crêpes from the batter, 1 to 2 minutes a side, and stack them.

In a wide frying pan melt the sugar over medium heat until it turns light amber, 3 to 5 minutes. Add the butter, then the orange juice and zest, and stir until the caramel dissolves into a smooth sauce, 2 to 3 minutes.
One at a time, lay each crêpe in the sauce for about 30 seconds, turn it, then fold it in half and in half again and push it to the side of the pan.
Pour in the liqueur and let it bubble 30 seconds to 1 minute. To flame it, tilt the pan away from you and light it with a long match, standing well back, and let the flames die out.
Serve 2 crêpes per plate with the sauce spooned over.

nutritionHighlights.note: The fresh orange juice and zest carry some vitamin C.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine makes the sauce from 50 g sugar, 60 g butter, two oranges and 3 cl Grand Marnier, soaking each crêpe about 30 seconds. Wikipédia names the beurre Suzette and Grand Marnier or curaçao, and ties the dish to Escoffier around 1890. The database holds a general liqueur, used for Grand Marnier.

recipes.name: Crêpes au Sucre
recipes.flavorProfile: Hot, thin, lacy crêpes with a smear of melting butter and a crunch of sugar, the plain street crêpe of France.
recipes.healthBenefit: A simple treat of white flour, butter and sugar with egg and milk in the batter for a little protein and calcium.
instructions: Heat a crêpe pan or 24 cm frying pan over medium high heat and wipe it with a little butter.
Pour in a small ladle of batter and tilt the pan to cover the base thinly. Cook 1 to 2 minutes, until the edge lifts and the underside is speckled gold, then flip and cook 30 seconds to 1 minute.
While the crêpe is still in the pan, rub a little butter over it and scatter about 1 tsp of sugar, with a few drops of lemon if you like.
Fold in half and then in half again and serve straight away. Repeat with the rest of the batter.

nutritionHighlights.note: The milk in the batter adds some calcium.

recipes.curationNote: Batter proportions follow Géraldine and the shared crêpe base. Wikipédia describes crêpes eaten hot with butter and sugar added once they are cooked, the everyday way and the one served at Chandeleur.

recipes.name: Profiteroles
recipes.flavorProfile: Crisp, hollow little choux puffs filled with cold vanilla ice cream and drowned in warm, glossy dark chocolate sauce.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat of butter, egg, cream and sugar; the dark chocolate adds a little iron and magnesium.
instructions: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Pipe the choux paste into 18 mounds about 3 cm across on a lined tray, spaced well apart.
Bake 25 to 30 minutes, until puffed, deep golden and light. Do not open the door for the first 20 minutes. Pierce each puff once and cool on a rack.
For the sauce, bring the cream to a simmer, pour it over the chocolate, wait 1 minute, then stir until smooth and stir in the butter.
Just before serving, split each puff and fill it with a small scoop of ice cream. Set 3 on each plate and pour the warm sauce over.

nutritionHighlights.note: The dark chocolate sauce adds a little iron.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia describes the profiterole as choux once filled with crème pâtissière and now usually with vanilla ice cream, covered in chocolate sauce; the English article ties the choux to Carême. Ice cream is listed as not in the database. Sauce is a standard dark chocolate and cream ganache, written from those descriptions because the search budget had run out.

components.note: enough for 12 fingers about 12 cm long

recipes.name: Éclairs au Chocolat
recipes.flavorProfile: Long, crisp choux fingers split with a cool, thick chocolate pastry cream and topped with a shiny chocolate fondant glaze.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich pastry of butter, egg, milk and sugar; the dark chocolate brings a little iron and magnesium and the pastry cream some calcium.

ingredients.cutPrep: chopped, stirred into the warm pastry cream

instructions: Make the crème pâtissière and, while it is still hot, stir in the chopped chocolate until melted. Cover the surface and chill at least 2 hours.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Pipe the choux paste into 12 fingers about 12 cm long and 2.5 cm wide on a lined tray.
Bake 40 to 50 minutes, until deep golden and dry, without opening the door in the first 25 minutes. Cool on a rack.
Make 2 or 3 small holes underneath each éclair and pipe in the chocolate cream until each feels heavy.

Warm the fondant with the cocoa and a little water over low heat to about 95°F (35°C), until it flows. Dip the top of each éclair, wipe the edge, and let it set 15 to 20 minutes. Keep chilled and eat within the day.

nutritionHighlights.note: The milk in the pastry cream adds calcium.
Chocolate in both the cream and glaze adds a little iron.

recipes.curationNote: olive pipes 10 to 12 éclairs at 12 cm and bakes them at 180°C for 40 to 50 minutes, glazing with 200 g fondant and a spoon of cocoa. Wikipédia describes a 12 to 14 cm choux filled with crème pâtissière and glazed with fondant, dating to around 1850 in Lyon. The filling here is the shared pastry cream with dark chocolate stirred in.

components.note: half a batch, piped as a 20 cm ring

recipes.name: Paris-Brest
recipes.flavorProfile: A wheel of crisp choux pastry scattered with toasted flaked almonds, split and piped full of a rich, nutty hazelnut praline butter cream.
recipes.healthBenefit: A very rich treat of butter, sugar and eggs; the almonds and hazelnuts add vitamin E and some magnesium.
instructions: For the praline, toast the hazelnuts and whole almonds at 325°F (160°C) for 10 to 12 minutes. Melt the sugar in a dry pan to an amber caramel, 6 to 8 minutes, stir in the warm nuts, and spread on a lined tray to harden. Break it up and blend 3 to 6 minutes, scraping down, to a smooth paste.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Pipe a ring of choux 20 cm across, then a second ring inside it and a third on top along the join. Brush with beaten egg and scatter the flaked almonds over.
Bake 40 to 45 minutes, until deep golden and firm, without opening the door for the first 25 minutes. Cool on a rack and slice in half horizontally.
Beat the soft butter until pale, 2 to 3 minutes, then beat in the cold crème pâtissière a spoonful at a time and then the praline paste, until smooth and light.
Pipe the praline cream in thick rosettes over the bottom ring, set the top on, and dust with icing sugar. Chill 30 minutes to 1 hour before slicing.

nutritionHighlights.note: Hazelnuts and almonds are among the richest food sources of vitamin E.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia describes a ring of choux topped with flaked almonds and filled with a praline mousseline (crème pâtissière beaten with butter and praline), created by Louis Durand around 1910 for the Paris to Brest bicycle race. Praline paste is made from the nuts here because the database has no praline; amounts are standard proportions, as the search budget had run out.

recipes.name: Madeleines
recipes.flavorProfile: Small shell-shaped butter cakes with crisp golden edges, a soft, fine, honeyed crumb, a hint of lemon and the classic hump on top.
recipes.healthBenefit: A small butter and sugar treat; one madeleine is a modest portion.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

ingredients.cutPrep: melted and cooled, plus a little for the tin

instructions: Whisk the eggs, sugar and honey until pale and foamy, 3 to 5 minutes. Stir in the lemon zest.
Fold in the flour, baking powder and salt, then the cooled melted butter, until smooth.
Cover and chill the batter at least 2 hours, or overnight. The cold batter against a hot oven gives the hump.
Butter and flour a madeleine tin. Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Fill each shell three quarters full.
Bake 4 minutes, then lower the oven to 350°F (180°C) and bake another 6 to 8 minutes, until golden at the edges and springy. Turn out at once and eat warm or the same day.

nutritionHighlights.note: The butter and eggs bring a little vitamin A.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine makes 15 madeleines from 2 eggs, 100 g sugar, a spoon of honey, 150 g flour, 125 g butter, baking powder and lemon zest, chilled 2 hours and started at 220°C. Wikipédia names Commercy in Lorraine and the same ingredients.

recipes.name: Financiers
recipes.flavorProfile: Small, moist almond cakes with a crisp golden crust and a chewy, nutty crumb tasting of browned butter.
recipes.healthBenefit: A butter and sugar treat; the ground almonds add vitamin E and some magnesium, and the egg whites a little protein.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

instructions: Melt the butter in a small pan over medium heat and cook 4 to 6 minutes, until it smells nutty and the solids at the bottom turn hazelnut brown. Strain and let it cool to warm.
Mix the icing sugar, ground almonds, flour and salt. Stir in the egg whites and vanilla until smooth, without beating in air.
Stir in the browned butter until glossy. Chill the batter 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Butter 8 financier or small rectangular moulds and fill them three quarters full.
Bake 15 to 18 minutes, until golden brown at the edges and springy in the centre. Cool 5 minutes, then turn out.
recipes.curationNote: Géraldine makes 8 from 100 g browned butter, 100 g icing sugar, 75 g ground almonds, 40 g flour and 3 whites, chilled 30 minutes and baked at 180°C. Wikipédia gives the same beurre noisette, almond powder, white and icing sugar cake, recorded by Lacam in 1865.

recipes.name: Île Flottante
recipes.flavorProfile: Soft clouds of poached meringue floating on cold vanilla custard, laced with threads of crisp amber caramel and toasted almonds.
recipes.healthBenefit: Lighter than it looks, since the meringue is mostly egg white, but the custard and caramel make it a sweet treat; the yolks bring choline and the milk calcium.

ingredients.cutPrep: kept at a bare simmer for poaching

instructions: Chill the crème anglaise at least 2 hours.
Whisk the whites with the salt to soft peaks, then add the icing sugar and whisk to firm, glossy peaks.
Bring a wide pan of water to a bare simmer. Drop in large spoonfuls of meringue, a few at a time, and poach 2 to 3 minutes, then turn them and poach 1 minute more. Lift onto a clean cloth to drain.
Pour the custard into 6 shallow bowls and set the meringues on top. Chill until serving.

For the caramel, heat the sugar and 30 ml water without stirring until amber, 6 to 8 minutes. Off the heat, drizzle it in thin threads over the meringues with a fork and scatter the toasted almonds over.

nutritionHighlights.note: Five egg whites give the meringue protein with almost no fat.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine poaches 5 whites beaten with 50 g icing sugar for about 3 minutes and 1 minute, floats them on a 5 yolk crème anglaise, and finishes with caramel and toasted almonds. Wikipédia treats île flottante and oeufs à la neige as one dessert and notes the whites are often poached in milk; water is used here so the poaching liquid is not counted as eaten.

recipes.name: Far Breton
recipes.flavorProfile: A dense, custardy, slightly chewy flan baked dark on top, studded with soft prunes and rich with salted Breton butter.
recipes.healthBenefit: A sweet treat, though made with milk rather than cream; the prunes bring fibre, potassium and vitamin K, and the eggs and milk add protein and calcium.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached
Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

ingredients.cutPrep: melted, plus a little for the dish

instructions: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Butter a 24 cm round or 20 by 30 cm baking dish generously and scatter the prunes in it.
Whisk the eggs with the sugar and salt, then whisk in the flour until smooth. Add the milk gradually, then the melted salted butter, to a thin batter. Rest it 30 minutes to 1 hour if you have time.
Pour the batter over the prunes.
Bake 40 to 50 minutes, until puffed and well browned on top and set in the centre; it sinks as it cools.
Cool to room temperature before slicing, or chill it, which firms the texture.

nutritionHighlights.note: A quarter kilo of prunes gives each slice a share of fibre.
The three quarters of a litre of milk adds calcium.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia lists eggs, sugar, flour, milk, salted butter and prunes, baked around 200°C for 30 to 45 minutes. The English article notes the prunes are not traditionally soaked in alcohol and the top bakes dark. Proportions are standard ones for a 24 cm dish, written from those descriptions because the search budget had run out.

recipes.name: Tarte au Citron
recipes.flavorProfile: A crisp, buttery sweet pastry shell filled with a smooth, sharp, silky lemon curd, tart first and then sweet.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat of butter, sugar and eggs; the fresh lemon brings vitamin C and the eggs protein and choline.

ingredients.cutPrep: zest of 2, juice of all, about 175 ml

instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Line a 23 cm tart tin with the pastry, prick it, line with paper and baking beans, and blind bake 15 minutes. Remove the beans and bake 5 to 10 minutes more, until golden. Cool.
Whisk the sugar, eggs and cornstarch in a saucepan, then whisk in the lemon juice and zest.
Cook over medium low heat, whisking all the time, until it thickens and the first bubbles break the surface, 5 to 8 minutes. Take off the heat.
Whisk in the butter a few cubes at a time until smooth and glossy. Strain if you want it very fine.
Pour into the cooled shell, smooth the top, and chill at least 4 hours before slicing.

nutritionHighlights.note: The juice of five lemons gives each slice some vitamin C.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine blind bakes a sweet pastry at 180°C and fills it with a curd of 150 g sugar, 4 eggs, 20 g cornstarch, 175 ml lemon juice with zest and 100 g butter, chilled at least 4 hours. Wikipédia describes the same pastry and lemon cream tart and its ties to Menton. Her pastry adds ground almonds; the shared pâte sucrée is used here.

recipes.name: Macarons
recipes.flavorProfile: Two smooth, crisp almond meringue shells with ruffled feet and a chewy centre, sandwiched with a dark chocolate ganache.
recipes.healthBenefit: A small sugary treat; the almonds add a little vitamin E, and one macaron is a light portion.
instructions: Sift the ground almonds and icing sugar together twice, discarding any coarse bits.
Whisk the whites with the salt to soft peaks, then add the sugar a little at a time and whisk to stiff, glossy peaks.
Fold the almond mixture into the meringue, then keep folding and pressing the batter against the bowl (the macaronage) until it falls from the spatula in a thick ribbon, 40 to 60 strokes.
Pipe 3 cm rounds on lined trays, rap the trays on the counter to release air, and leave them 30 minutes to 1 hour until a skin forms and they are no longer sticky.

Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C) and bake one tray at a time 12 to 15 minutes, until the shells lift cleanly. Cool fully. For the ganache, pour the simmering cream over the chocolate, stir smooth, and cool until pipeable. Sandwich the shells in pairs and chill them 24 hours so the centres soften.

nutritionHighlights.note: The ground almonds bring a little vitamin E.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia describes the Paris macaron as equal weights of almond powder and icing sugar folded into whipped whites and sugar, two shells joined by ganache, made famous by Ladurée. The English article sets out the French and Italian meringue methods, the macaronage and the skin before baking. The French meringue method is used; amounts are standard proportions, written from those descriptions because the search budget had run out.

recipes.name: Crème Caramel
recipes.flavorProfile: A cool, wobbling vanilla custard turned out under a pool of thin, bittersweet amber caramel.
recipes.healthBenefit: A lighter custard than crème brûlée, made with milk rather than cream; the eggs bring protein and choline and the milk calcium, though the caramel adds sugar.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D

instructions: Heat the sugar and water without stirring until a deep amber caramel, 6 to 9 minutes. Pour it at once into 6 ramekins and tilt to coat the bases.
Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C). Warm the milk with the vanilla pod and seeds until steaming, then infuse 10 minutes.
Whisk the eggs, yolks and sugar together without making foam, pour in the warm milk, and strain.
Pour the custard over the caramel and set the ramekins in a deep tray with hot water halfway up their sides. Bake 35 to 45 minutes, until set at the edge with a slight wobble in the middle.
Cool, then chill at least 4 hours. Run a knife around each one and turn out onto a plate so the caramel runs down.

nutritionHighlights.note: Half a litre of milk adds calcium.
Eggs and milk give each custard some protein.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia describes eggs, milk, sugar and a vanilla pod baked in a water bath in caramel-lined moulds; the English article adds the turning out. Proportions are standard ones for six ramekins, written from those descriptions because the search budget had run out.

components.note: half a batch, rolled into one large thin sheet

recipes.name: Mille-Feuille
recipes.flavorProfile: Three sheets of crisp, caramelized puff pastry layered with thick vanilla pastry cream, topped with white fondant feathered with chocolate.
recipes.healthBenefit: A very rich pastry of butter, flour, milk, eggs and sugar; the pastry cream adds some calcium.
instructions: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Roll the puff pastry into a 30 by 40 cm sheet about 2 mm thin, lay it on a lined tray, prick it all over and chill 15 minutes.

Lay a sheet of paper and a second tray on the pastry so it rises evenly. Bake 15 to 20 minutes, then remove the top tray, dust with the icing sugar and bake 5 to 8 minutes more, until deep golden and glossy. Cool.
Trim and cut into 3 equal strips. Beat the cold crème pâtissière smooth and pipe half over one strip, cover with the second, pipe the rest, and set the third strip on top, flat side up.
Warm the fondant to about 95°F (35°C) and spread it over the top. Pipe thin lines of melted chocolate across and drag a knife through them in alternating directions to feather.
Chill 1 hour to set, then cut into 8 with a serrated knife.

nutritionHighlights.note: The milk in the pastry cream adds calcium.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia describes three layers of puff pastry with two of crème pâtissière, glazed with fondant marbled with chocolate, and credits Seugnot with the modern form in 1867. Amounts and the pressed bake are standard method, written from those descriptions because the search budget had run out.

recipes.name: Tarte aux Fraises
recipes.flavorProfile: A crisp sweet pastry shell spread with cool vanilla pastry cream and crowded with fresh, juicy strawberries.
recipes.healthBenefit: A treat of pastry, cream and sugar, lighter than many because of the fresh fruit; the strawberries bring plenty of vitamin C and folate.
instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Line a 23 cm tart tin with the pastry, prick it, line with paper and baking beans, and blind bake 15 minutes. Remove the beans and bake 5 to 10 minutes more, until golden. Cool completely.
Beat the cold crème pâtissière until smooth and spread it evenly in the shell.
Arrange the strawberries close together over the cream, points up.
Chill up to 2 hours and dust with icing sugar just before serving. It is best eaten the day it is made.

nutritionHighlights.note: Half a kilo of fresh strawberries gives each slice a good share of vitamin C.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine fills sweet almond pastry shells, baked at 175°C, with crème pâtissière and 300 g strawberries for 8 tartlets; this is the same tart in one 23 cm shell with more fruit. Her flan pâtissier page sets out crème pâtissière as the base for tarts. A second, independent source could not be opened because the search budget had run out.

recipes.name: Canelés
recipes.flavorProfile: Small fluted cakes with a thick, dark, almost burnt caramelized crust around a soft, custardy centre scented with rum and vanilla.
recipes.healthBenefit: A small sugary treat; the milk and eggs add a little protein and calcium.

ingredients.baseName: Milk, whole, 3.25% milkfat, with added vitamin D
Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

instructions: Bring the milk to a boil with the vanilla pod and seeds and the 50 g butter, then take off the heat.
Mix the sugar and flour, then stir in the egg and yolks. Pour in the hot milk gradually, stirring without beating, until smooth. Cool, add the rum, and remove the pod.
Cover and chill the batter 24 to 48 hours.
Heat the oven to 465°F (240°C). Brush copper or silicone canelé moulds with the melted butter. Stir the batter gently and fill the moulds to 1 cm from the top.
Bake 10 minutes, then lower to 350°F (180°C) and bake 45 to 55 minutes, until the crusts are a deep mahogany. Turn out at once and cool on a rack; they are crispest within a few hours.

nutritionHighlights.note: Half a litre of milk spread over 16 cakes adds a little calcium.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine uses 500 ml milk, vanilla, 225 g sugar, 125 g flour, an egg, 3 yolks, 50 g butter and 3 tbsp rum, rested 24 to 48 hours and baked at 240°C then 180°C. Wikipédia ties the canelé to Bordeaux, rum and vanilla, and copper moulds coated with beeswax and butter; butter alone is used here.

recipes.name: Poires Belle Hélène
recipes.flavorProfile: Whole pears poached soft in vanilla syrup, served cold with vanilla ice cream and hot, glossy dark chocolate sauce poured over at the table.
recipes.healthBenefit: A sweet treat; the pears bring fibre and potassium, and the dark chocolate a little iron and magnesium.

ingredients.cutPrep: firm, such as Williams, peeled with stems on
for the syrup, most of it stays in the pan

instructions: Bring the water, sugar, lemon juice and vanilla pod to a boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves.

Rub the peeled pears with lemon, lower them into the syrup and keep it at a gentle simmer 10 to 25 minutes, depending on ripeness, until a knife slides in easily. Cool the pears in the syrup and chill.
For the sauce, bring the cream to a simmer, pour it over the chocolate, wait 1 minute, stir until smooth, and stir in the butter. Keep it warm.
Stand each drained pear in a bowl beside a scoop of ice cream, pour the hot chocolate sauce over and scatter with the toasted almonds.

nutritionHighlights.note: A whole pear per serving brings a fair amount of fibre.
The dark chocolate adds some magnesium.

recipes.curationNote: Géraldine poaches 4 pears in 1 litre of water with 250 g sugar and lemon for 10 to 25 minutes and serves them with warm chocolate and almonds. Wikipédia sets the classic version: pears poached in vanilla syrup with vanilla ice cream and hot dark chocolate sauce, named by Escoffier after Offenbach's 1864 opera. Ice cream is listed as not in the database; only part of the syrup sugar is eaten, so the totals run high on sugar.

components.note: about 2 cups, cold, flavoured with rum

recipes.name: Gâteau Basque
recipes.flavorProfile: A crumbly, buttery almond shortbread crust baked golden around a thick layer of rum and vanilla pastry cream.
recipes.healthBenefit: A rich treat of butter, sugar and eggs; the ground almonds add a little vitamin E.

ingredients.baseName: Wheat flour, white, all-purpose, enriched, unbleached

ingredients.cutPrep: one for the dough, one for glazing

instructions: Beat the butter and sugar until creamy, then beat in the egg, one yolk and the lemon zest. Mix in the flour, ground almonds, baking powder and salt until just combined. Divide into two thirds and one third, wrap, and chill 1 to 2 hours.
Stir the rum into the cold crème pâtissière.
Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C). Butter a 22 to 24 cm cake tin. Roll the larger piece of dough 5 mm thick between sheets of paper and line the base and sides of the tin.
Spread the cream in it, roll the smaller piece into a lid, lay it over and press the edges to seal. Brush with the beaten last yolk and score a crosshatch with a fork.
Bake 40 to 50 minutes, until deep golden. Cool fully in the tin before slicing.

nutritionHighlights.note: The ground almonds add a little vitamin E.
The milk in the pastry cream adds calcium.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia describes a sablé dough filled with black cherry jam from Itxassou or with an almond or rum crème pâtissière, credited to Marianne Hirigoyen of Cambo. The English article notes the cream version is marked with a crosshatch and the cherry one with the Basque cross. The cream version is written here; dough amounts are standard proportions, as the search budget had run out.

recipes.name: Kouign-Amann
recipes.flavorProfile: A round, flaky, buttery cake of laminated bread dough with salted butter and sugar caramelized into a sticky, crackling, salty-sweet crust.
recipes.healthBenefit: A very rich treat, close to a third butter and a third sugar by weight; a thin slice is plenty.

ingredients.baseName: Grains, wheat flour, white, bread flour

ingredients.cutPrep: cold, Breton demi-sel, plus a little for the tin

instructions: Dissolve the yeast in the water and mix with the flour and salt. Knead 5 to 8 minutes to a smooth dough. Cover and rise 1 hour, until doubled.
Beat the cold salted butter flat between sheets of paper into a 15 cm square. Roll the dough into a 30 cm square, set the butter in the middle and fold the corners over it to enclose it.

Roll into a long rectangle and fold in three. Chill 20 to 30 minutes. Roll and fold again, scattering a third of the sugar over before folding. Repeat twice more, until all the sugar is in, chilling between turns if the butter softens.
Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C). Roll the dough into a round about 24 cm across, fold the edges in, and press it into a buttered 24 cm tin. Leave it 20 to 30 minutes.
Bake 50 minutes to 1 hour, until deep amber and caramelized. Turn out onto a rack after 5 minutes, before the caramel sets in the tin. Eat warm or the same day.

nutritionHighlights.note: The salted butter carries vitamin A.

recipes.curationNote: Wikipédia gives the classic ratio of about 40 percent bread dough, 30 percent salted butter and 30 percent sugar, baked about an hour at 160°C, created by Yves-René Scordia in Douarnenez around 1860; the English article confirms the laminated dough. Weights follow that ratio for one 24 cm cake; method is standard lamination, written from those descriptions because the search budget had run out.
